name: Bianca Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead the glass-bottle forming line. My two-year technical diploma covered mould settings, and I can hear a bad forming cycle before the neck gauge catches it. I like a clean bottle neck; hot glass splinters after a jam are what I dread.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works variable bakery shifts. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. I am one of the best setters here, but the lead wage is low for this job and there are few similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to sort defect photographs, then check against cooled glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bottle crew the AI chart helps find a weak neck on the glass line, but somebody still has to pull a cooled bottle and test it. If AI stays modest, that sounds like our current work. We should ask why the lead rate stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a two-year technical diploma and lead the glass forming crew, yet our plant pays below the normal lead rate. My partner's bakery hours vary, our two children are in school, and the mortgage takes most pay. We have only three weeks of expenses saved and few similar factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the bottle moulds and measuring the neck of the first cooled bottle each run. I already use AI daily to sort defect photographs, and I'll keep checking its pattern against glass samples. I'll ask the manager for the written lead-rate table before the next pay review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even without a dramatic new machine. Three weeks saved is a small answer to a large mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bottle fault did the chart miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday the AI chart missed a fine seam crack near the lip because the bottle turned in the photograph. I held that pallet and asked a colleague to test another bottle. A clean defect chart cannot make a cracked bottle safe for a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a slow bakery week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery cuts my partner's weekday hours when orders slow. We pay the mortgage first and then school meals, which leaves little for a broken fridge. I would use a full-pay month to add a little new money to the reserve.

Our crew still needs a **cooled-bottle test** before shipping a pallet.
think: My **lead skill** has not brought the usual lead rate.
Three weeks saved and **variable bakery hours** leave the mortgage exposed.
do: **Keep** checking first cooled bottles and measuring glass necks.
**Request** the written lead-rate table before the next pay review.
**Add** new full-pay wages to the reserve after bills.
feel: **Anxious** about existing low pay and a thin reserve.

fieldNote: Bianca **uses AI daily** on defect photos but trusts cooled samples and a colleague’s physical test.

steps.text: Keep setting glass moulds and test first cooled bottle each run
Ask manager for written glass-line lead pay table
Save new full-pay glass wages after mortgage and school bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may plan bottle orders and inspect photographs before robots can change hot moulds. I would ask the plant for a paid trial with real rejects before shortening any crew rota. A fast camera chart has to catch cracked bottle necks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the new inspection screen, but management might use it to reduce paid checking time on the line. One lost shift would hurt our mortgage with only three weeks saved. My partner's bakery wage cannot make up a regular glass-line day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for the proposed paid inspection minutes and compare them with last month's slips. If the plant offers a paid guarded trial with a trainer on new camera controls, I'll learn to reject cracked sample bottles. I'll also practise a new AI comparison of bottle-neck photos on anonymised test batches, checking every finding against a cooled sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about lost paid time, though I want to test the camera. I can tell management a missed crack has a cost as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the camera safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feed a known cracked test bottle through the camera and see if it rejects it. The trainer would show the safe stop and keep our hands clear of moving glass. I would not use a live pallet for my first lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which roster detail matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid minutes matter more than how many bottles a report counts. If the proposed rota removes a shift, I would ask for the base-rate change in writing. Our three-week reserve cannot pay a month's missing wage.

think: I can learn **new controls**, but may lose paid checking time.

S1.quote: A fast camera chart has to catch cracked bottle necks.
fieldNote: Her **new AI practice** extends beyond current defect sorting to bottle-neck comparisons.
The **camera-control lesson** depends on offered paid guarded time with a trainer and test bottles.

steps.text: Compare proposed paid glass inspection time with recent wage slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI could plan bottle orders by 2028, then capable robots around 2031 could change moulds and inspect glass. We need a written staffing date before anyone gives up paid hours. I'd ask what happens to the lead crew first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots do the hands-on glass work. I expect most of our mould crew could lose shifts, including me, and my partner's bakery wage will not cover the mortgage. Three weeks saved is barely one pay cycle. I already lie awake after a short bakery rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask for a written mould-crew plan and any paid quality posts. If a funded paid-time certificate in glass testing comes with guarded practice and a real seat, I'll enrol. If my hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local production work only if regular pay and school hours cover our bills; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local glass-testing jobs under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can learn a new test, but I cannot teach the mortgage to wait while a course finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must glass-testing training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A practical test should include a bottle with a hairline neck crack and one with an uneven wall. I'd stop the conveyor and measure both under a trainer's eye. If that practice is unpaid, I cannot take the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes another production post viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fallback job needs an actual local posting with safe duties and a base wage we can live on. I would compare the shift start with school drop-off and the bakery rota. A promise of overtime would not be enough.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before robots handle glass around 2031.
The plant should give the crew a **written staffing date**.
think: At **48**, I expect major mould-crew hour loss.
Three weeks saved and **variable bakery pay** cannot carry the mortgage.
do: **Ask** plant for written crew and paid quality-role plans.
**Enrol** if funded paid guarded glass-testing place offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local production if cut or testing if qualified; pay and school hours must fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household worry.
S2.quote: I can learn a new test, but I cannot teach the mortgage to wait while a course finishes.
fieldNote: Her **thin reserve** and variable partner wage make the expected crew cut an immediate household threat.
The **production fallback** needs no certificate; a separate testing application follows funded paid guarded training and qualification.

steps.text: Ask plant for written mould staffing and paid quality posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might plan bottles by 2031, and capable robots could change moulds around 2034. Five years can buy paid practical instruction while the line still runs. I would want an actual quality vacancy beside the course notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots reach the hot line. A technical diploma and lead experience may help me qualify for inspection, but few glass plants are nearby. Full wages for five years could grow the reserve if the plant keeps its orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put new money from each full-pay month into our reserve after school and mortgage bills. I'll ask the plant for covered fees, paid release and guarded practice in a recognized glass-inspection course. If it offers a real seat, I'll enrol; once qualified, if mould hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local inspection roles only if the base wage and travel fit the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's narrow buffer and later crew cuts. Five years lets me verify the money before I leave a paid lead shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the inspection exam test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection exam should make me measure a thin bottle wall and reject a batch with a cracked neck. I would want the assessor beside the stopped conveyor. A glass-inspection certificate from photographs alone would not make me safe on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a vacancy worth applying to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the posting to state its regular rate and the actual plant location. If the only job is a long drive at lower pay, the mortgage and school runs might not fit. I would keep looking while I earn.

Few **local glass plants** and thin savings still limit choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan bottle orders by 2036 and capable robots could run moulds around 2039. A decade gives our children time to grow, but my plant still needs a plan in writing. I would ask for real training seats early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but I cannot budget as if the mortgage is gone. My low lead wage and three-week reserve still make this year's bills tight, whatever the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the glass line and put new money from full-pay months into savings after bills. I'll ask the equipment supplier for the exact funded fees, paid time and guarded practice of its maintenance apprenticeship. If a real seat is offered, I'll take it; after qualifying, if my mould hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local maintenance jobs only where base pay and travel cover our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current bills, with enough warning to check an apprenticeship carefully. A 2039 robot date does not make this month's glass-line wage larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the supplier apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a trainer to show how to isolate a mould changer, measure worn parts and restart on test glass. If the supplier only offers a demonstration, I would ask for another place. Paid supervised work is the point of the apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the maintenance job workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local maintenance job would need a posted rate and named shifts. If the travel leaves my partner handling every school pickup and the wage is lower, I'd keep the glass role while searching. We would discuss it at home first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut the glass crew before our household can bridge a month. A written plan, an offered funded paid practical seat and a posted safe local job at enough base pay would help. I would compare school hours before applying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the first bottle after a robot changes the mould. Glass looks clear until a thin neck cracks in someone's hand.

headlineQuote: Glass looks clear until a thin neck cracks in someone's hand.
portrait: **Bianca**, 43, is a senior glass-forming lead with a two-year technical diploma and strong practical skill.
She and her bakery-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage on low pay with three weeks saved.
Her **centre outlook** favors real numbers, while daily AI use helps her sort defect photos without replacing physical tests.
Fast robots make her **alarmed** about crew cuts; few local plants make offered paid training and posted jobs important.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable glass-forming robots around 2031 and cut household wages before savings grow.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, offered funded paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient base pay would help.
